analysis.one_liner: Makes large internet and tech companies help fund rural and low-income phone and internet subsidies.
analysis.headline: Despite bipartisan sponsorship, the bill never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Commerce Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the FCC to make large broadband companies and big tech platforms — search engines, social media, streaming services, cloud providers — pay into the Universal Service Fund, which today is funded almost entirely by traditional phone companies and shows up as a fee on customers' phone bills. Spreading that fee across more payers would ease the burden on ordinary phone customers. It would also create a new subsidy stream for broadband providers serving expensive rural areas, limited to one subsidized provider per area.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who pay the Universal Service Fund surcharge on their phone bills, since the cost would be spread across big tech and broadband companies instead of concentrated on telephone customers. Low-income households in the Lifeline program, schools, libraries, and rural health clinics that the fund supports would benefit from a more stable funding base, and rural residents could gain from the new high-cost broadband support mechanism. Rural broadband providers that qualify as eligible telecommunications carriers would gain a dedicated federal subsidy.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Phone customers; rural areas and broadband users

how_it_helps.text: Expands the Universal Service Fund's contribution base so large broadband providers and big tech edge providers — digital advertising, search engines, social media, streaming, app stores, cloud computing, videoconferencing, gaming, and e-commerce — share costs now carried almost entirely by telephone companies, whose customers pay the fee through their bills.

Exempts smaller companies: edge providers that carried under 3% of U.S. broadband traffic and earned under $5 billion in U.S. revenue, and any provider whose contribution would be trivial, so the burden falls on the largest platforms.

Requires the FCC to build a new high-cost support mechanism paying broadband providers for expenses they cannot recover from customers in rural areas where market forces do not support service, with support limited to one carrier per area.

analysis.who_pays: Large technology platforms above the bill's size thresholds ($5 billion in U.S. revenue and 3% of U.S. broadband traffic) and large broadband providers would owe new Universal Service Fund contributions. Some of those costs would likely be passed on to users through higher subscription prices or more advertising, and the FCC — not the bill — would decide exactly how much each company pays.
analysis.who_pays_short: Big tech platforms and large broadband providers

drawbacks.text: Fees charged to search engines, social media, streaming, and cloud services would likely be passed through to consumers as higher prices or more ads — meaning the people the bill says it is helping could end up paying part of the cost anyway.
The new rural support mechanism allows only one subsidized carrier per area, locking in a single government-funded provider and blocking competitors from serving the same ground.
The bill never requires telephone companies to pass their reduced contributions along as lower customer bills, so the promised consumer relief depends entirely on FCC rules and industry behavior.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Spreading the Universal Service Fund fee off phone bills and onto the biggest internet companies is a real, if modest, win for consumers, since the current fee is a flat surcharge that hits low-income households hardest. But the gains are uncertain: tech companies can pass fees to their users, phone companies face no obligation to cut their customers' bills, and the one-subsidized-carrier-per-area rule trades competition for a rural subsidy. The bill was also never workshopped in committee, so none of these design questions were ever tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Commerce Committee for over a year without a hearing or vote and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Markwayne Mullin introduced the bill on November 15, 2023, joined by Senators Mark Kelly and Mike Crapo, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
That referral was the last action the bill ever received: the committee held no hearing, took no vote, and the Senate never considered it before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted six cosponsors, five Republicans and one Democrat, but that support never translated into committee action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large tech platforms — search, social media, streaming, and cloud companies — are better off because the bill died, since they avoided new Universal Service Fund fees. Telephone customers are worse off, because the surcharge they pay on their phone bills stayed exactly where it was.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big tech platforms that avoided new fees

for.name: Sen. Markwayne Mullin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited a bipartisan group of cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Mark Kelly
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only Democratic support.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation (Chair Maria Cantwell)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill stayed at the referral stage for the entire 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Republican lead sponsor with one Democratic and five Republican cosponsors — but the bill never reached a vote, so no vote split exists.

industries.industry: Big tech platforms (search, social media, streaming, cloud, e-commerce)
industries.note: Companies over $5 billion in U.S. revenue carrying at least 3% of U.S. broadband traffic would have owed new Universal Service Fund contributions. Their interest in killing the bill ran against consumers' interest in lower phone-bill fees, and any fees they paid could resurface as higher prices or more ads.

The bill creates a dedicated high-cost subsidy for their unrecoverable rural expenses, limited to one carrier per area. That guarantee entrenches a single government-funded provider in each rural territory.

They are the only contributors to the Universal Service Fund today, so adding broadband and tech payers would dilute their share of a fund whose benefits, including the rural high-cost program, they also draw on.

Cable and fiber companies above the thresholds would pay new contributions, but qualifying carriers would also be eligible for the new rural high-cost support and would benefit from subsidies that make their rural networks viable.
